prize_parts.citation: for their theory of how lobbying and electoral incentives shape trade policy, making protection an equilibrium outcome of political-economy forces

statement.case_for: I keep B013 with Helpman and Grossman as a single-part prize. What changed after round 1 is the citation and my alternatives, not the ballot or the names. I narrow the citation to the shortlisted achievement, trade policy and special-interest politics, and drop the growth-and-trade clause I used in my opening. The ballot entry does not cover that strand, and Krusell's narrower wording is cleaner. It also keeps the citation away from the ground the 2008 prize covered. The core case is unchanged. Grossman and Helpman turned protection from an exogenous wedge into an equilibrium outcome of lobbying and electoral incentives. The result is a compact model with sharp, estimable predictions about which sectors are protected and how. It has been taken to data and used in work on tariff structures and trade agreements for three decades. The credit sits with a stable two-person partnership and jointly authored core papers, which is the cleanest attribution among the trade candidates and one of the cleanest on the list. I weigh most heavily theory built to explain observed policy patterns and then tested against them. The weak point is the second half of that standard, the mixed empirical record, and I do not wave it away. I do not treat Krusell agreeing with me as evidence of merit, because our overlap is long and our views are correlated. On the chair's Helpman question, I would credit him for this achievement, not for firm heterogeneity. The 2008 prize concerned scale economies and trade patterns, which is a different object from the political economy of policy formation, so I see room for either trade award and no bar against B013.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Tests of the specific Protection for Sale predictions give mixed results, and some structural estimates imply parameter values that are hard to interpret. Much of the influence is on how trade policy is modelled, not on a settled finding about the world. Part of the field was recognised in 2008, and Helpman is also credited on B041, so a committee that prefers a firm-heterogeneity prize would compete for the same laureate. The conceptual influence is also less easy to measure than the documented policy reach of B038 or B002. After the exchange I think B038 is the strongest rival on exactly the axis where B013 is weakest. B038 has a design that is credible, replicated and now standard, with an attribution that has largely converged on Autor, Dorn and Hanson. If a majority judged that tested evidence should outweigh foundational theory, I would not call that unreasonable. I did not rank B038 in my opening and have updated my alternatives to reflect it.

responses.point: Teorell did not rank B013 and finds the measurement and empirical support for the lobbying-contribution mechanism thin, so he would need more evidence of a transformative empirical effect.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection to my choice and I concede its core. The functional form of the lobbying mechanism has not been confirmed as cleanly as the framework is used, and a prize should not rest on influence alone. Where I differ is on what the evidence shows. The framework gave empirical work a structure that did not exist before. Researchers could ask which sectors are protected, how much weight governments put on welfare against contributions, and how trade agreements change this. A model that organises and sharpens later testing, even when its parameter estimates are contested, has done what theory is supposed to do. That is a real discount, and it is why I now treat B013 as only modestly ahead of B038 and B012, not clearly ahead. I rely on general knowledge here, not an independent review of the tariff-structure literature.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 first. He treats Melitz (2003) as a single, checkable discovery with two decades of confirmation, and sees B013 as a rival configuration for Helpman that mainly changed how policy formation is modelled.
responses.response: I agree the two trade configurations compete for Helpman and are not complements. I also accept that B041 changed how trade is measured and estimated, which gives it reach that B013 does not have. My difference with him is attribution. He acknowledges the competing claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are outside the ballot, and that is a structural problem a Melitz-Helpman citation cannot resolve. The Grossman-Helpman pairing has no such gap. I would not oppose a Melitz award on merit, and Andersson's and Hassler's Melitz-alone fallback is coherent. On a common standard of clean credit plus maturity, I still rank the Grossman-Helpman programme as the more complete body of work. I do not count the possibility of a later Melitz recognition against B013.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B013 to B038 after round 1. He still holds B013 as a close alternative and says it needs a narrower, clearer rationale, and he cites the mixed empirical record and the overlap with B041.
responses.response: His move is informative because he started from the same place I did and weighted the empirical record more heavily. I took his call for a narrower rationale on board and have confined the citation to political economy and trade policy. I would not go further and describe B013 as a lesser candidate. The question between us is how to weigh a mature, cleanly attributed, mixed-evidence framework against a younger design whose magnitudes are still disputed. The empirical standard he applies in his own work is the right one, and I do not dismiss it. I still think the foundational depth and the unusually clean credit are enough to keep B013 first. I would be more comfortable if he and I agreed on what would count as sufficient empirical support, since we seem to differ more on that than on the facts.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 first for new data combined with an explanatory framework, more than a decade of replication, and a design now standard in the field. She ranks B013 only sixth.
responses.response: I take her argument that the standing of B038 rests on years of independent scrutiny, and that a contribution which survived its own methodological critique has earned some credit for that. It is why I have moved B038 into my alternatives in place of B030. My remaining reservations are the ones I raised in round 1, and they are now narrower than before. The ballot entry bundles the task framework and the China-shock evidence, and the citation has to avoid claiming the task lineage for the trio. If the committee restricts the citation to local labour-market adjustment to trade and technology exposure, as Enflo and Fredriksson propose, much of that objection falls away. Then the choice with B013 is mostly a judgement about whether tested empirical design or foundational theory should weigh more, and I do not claim that judgement is free of my own field's standards.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B012 first. He presents Kiyotaki and Moore as a precise, mature mechanism with a clean two-person core, supported by the 2008 crisis, and accepts that the 2022 overlap and mixed empirical identification remain risks.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person attribution and on three decades of use, and B012 stays as my first alternative. I still place it behind B013 for the same reason Boppart himself lists as a risk. The collateral channel has been hard to identify directly, and the 2022 prize covered neighbouring ground on banks and crises, so I see less distance from earlier recognition than for the political-economy strand of trade. This is a modest difference. His observation that events after 2008 bore out the mechanism is a stronger confirmation than anything available for Protection for Sale, and I count that for B012. I do not think the gap between B012 and B013 is large. I would not claim more than that.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give mixed empirical support for the specific Protection for Sale predictions against the framework's role in organising later empirical work. This is the single largest risk to my preferred part.
Whether the committee prefers one Helpman award or two competing trade configurations. A Grossman-Helpman award would likely foreclose a Melitz-Helpman award, or at least change it to Melitz alone.
Whether the 2008 trade prize reduces appetite for a second trade-theory award, even though the political-economy strand is distinct.

Whether tested empirical programmes such as B038 should outrank foundational theory with a mixed record under common criteria. My own research habit of testing theory against hand-collected data may bias me toward either side of that comparison.

My assessments of B012 and B038 rest on general knowledge without independent verification, so the order of my alternatives is tentative. The same applies to my reading of the empirical literature on B013.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance and private equity, and my listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson, Martinsson, Thomann) do not appear among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot entry, including B013, B012 and B038. I have a long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, and Krusell also ranks B013 first. I treat that agreement as disclosure only and do not count it as support for merit. I engaged Hassler's B041 position on scientific grounds. I share an SSE affiliation with Andersson, Dreber Almenberg and Friberg, which is a colleague connection and not a candidate connection. My Vice Presidency of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and my current-term status are institutional facts with no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
